blocks.text: 1. Multi-Agent Systems
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163277-556452405.png

Memory closed the trio of planning, reflection, and memory as capabilities a single agent builds on top of tool calling. Multi-Agent Systems, several specialized agents coordinating toward a shared goal, extends that idea from one capable agent to several agents working together.
It splits one broad task across separate agents, each responsible for a narrower piece of it.
2. One Generalist Agent Versus Several Specialists

blocks.alt: One Generalist Agent Versus Several Specialists
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163277-756450123.png
A single agent handling every kind of sub-task must be capable at all of them at once, unlike decomposing the goal into steps assigned to a plan in Planning.
Several specialized agents instead each handle only the sub-task they are built for.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Architecture","How capability is organized"],"rows":[["Single generalist agent","One agent capable at every kind of sub-task"],["Multi-agent system","Several agents, each specialized in one sub-task"]]}

blocks.text: 3. A Coordinator Assigns Work To Specialists

blocks.alt: A Coordinator Assigns Work To Specialists
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163278-201812564.png
A coordinator agent decides which specialist agent handles which piece of the task, much like routing between modules in Modular RAG.
It is a dynamic version of that same routing idea, now routing between whole agents rather than just modules.
4. Agents Pass Results To One Another

blocks.alt: Agents Pass Results To One Another
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163539-230947946.png
One agent's completed output often becomes the next agent's input, similar to how hop two uses the first hop's result in Multi-Hop RAG.
It is the same dependency chain, just between agents instead of retrieval hops.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A research agent's gathered findings passed directly to a writing agent is the same input-depends-on-prior-output pattern as hop two using the first hop's result, just applied between two whole agents.

blocks.text: 5. Each Agent Can Have Its Own Tools And Memory

blocks.alt: Each Agent Can Have Its Own Tools And Memory
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163539-696269003.png
Each specialist agent can be equipped with only the specific tools its own role needs, extending the idea that tool calling is the foundation of agentic RAG from Tool Calling.
A retrieval specialist and a summarization specialist do not need each other's tools.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Agent role","Tools it needs"],"rows":[["Retrieval specialist","Search and retrieval tools only"],["Summarization specialist","Text condensing tools only, not search tools"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Reflection Across Agents, Not Just Within One
A reviewer agent can evaluate another agent's output before it is passed along, extending reflection on the final answer from Reflection to run between agents rather than within just one.
Reflection applies between agents, not only within a single agent's own loop.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A dedicated reviewer agent checking a writing agent's draft before it reaches the user extends the same evaluative check as reflection on the final answer, now applied between two separate agents.

blocks.text: 7. Coordination Overhead Grows With Agent Count

blocks.alt: Coordination Overhead Grows With Agent Count
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163540-654589317.png
Every additional specialist agent adds its own coordination overhead, the same tradeoff as each added step costing latency in Advanced RAG.
More agents does not automatically mean a better result.
8. Failures In One Agent Can Stall The Others
One agent that produces a wrong or stalled result blocks every agent waiting on it, the same propagation risk as an error in an early hop in Multi-Hop RAG.
It is the same propagation risk, now across agents instead of hops.
9. Recognizing When Multi-Agent Systems Earn Their Coordination Overhead

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Multi-Agent Systems Earn Their Coordination Overhead
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441163540-590817035.png
Tasks with distinct, specialized sub-parts benefit from separate agents.
A task one capable agent already handles well, by contrast, does not need multiple coordinated agents.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Splitting a task across many agents when one capable generalist agent already handles it well.
Giving every agent the same broad set of tools instead of scoping tools to each agent's role.
Skipping a reviewer or reflection step between agents, letting a bad output pass through unchecked.
Underestimating how much coordination overhead grows as more specialist agents are added.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-agent systems split one broad task across several agents, each specialized in a sub-task.
A single generalist agent must be capable at everything; specialists each handle one narrower piece.
A coordinator agent decides which specialist handles which piece, a dynamic form of routing.
One agent's completed output often becomes the next agent's input, the same dependency chain as hops.
Each specialist agent can be equipped with only the specific tools its own role actually needs.
A reviewer agent can apply reflection across agents, not only within a single agent's own loop.
Every additional specialist agent adds its own coordination overhead; more agents is not automatically better.
One agent's wrong or stalled result can block every other agent waiting on it.
